Microbiological Research.title: Forsythiaside A enhances host defense against Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia by modulating gut microbiota-derived indole-3-lactic acid and AhR signaling.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia poses a major clinical challenge due to its high pathogenicity and rising antibiotic resistance. Forsythiae Fructus has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine for treating lung diseases, particularly bacterial pneumonia. However, whether its major bioactive constituent, forsythiaside A (FA), exerts therapeutic effects against P. aeruginosa-induced pneumonia and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we evaluated the protective effect of FA in a PAO1-induced murine pneumonia model. Although FA exhibited negligible direct antibacterial activity in vitro, it markedly alleviated pulmonary infection and lung injury in vivo, indicating a host-directed protection. Furthermore, depletion of the gut microbiota by antibiotics attenuated the therapeutic effect of FA, whereas fecal microbiota transplantation from FA-treated mice improved disease outcomes, highlighting the crucial role of the gut microbiota in FA mediated protection. 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics analysis showed that FA reshaped the gut microbiota, leading to the enrichment of Limosilactobacillus reuteri and increased production of the tryptophan-derived metabolite indole-3-lactic acid (ILA). Mechanistically, ILA activated AhR signaling pathway in macrophages to upregulate CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 expressions, which in turn triggered intracellular ROS generation and ultimately enhanced macrophage-mediated bacterial killing. Moreover, combining FA with polymyxin B improved therapeutic efficacy against P. aeruginosa-induced pneumonia. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that FA protects against P. aeruginosa pneumonia through a novel gut microbiota dependent, host-directed mechanism, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for bacterial pneumonia.

EMBO Reports.title: DCAF15-ANKIB1 E3 super-complex licenses NLRP3 inflammasome activation via KAT5 serine ubiquitination.
EMBO Reports.abstract: Aberrant activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome is a key driver of inflammatory diseases such as sepsis. The acetyltransferase KAT5 acetylates NLRP3 and promotes the subsequent full activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, but the mechanism by which KAT5 exerts its acetyltransferase activity to acetylate NLRP3 is not well characterized. Here, we identify that the E3 ligase DCAF15 plays a critical role in positively regulating NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Specifically, DCAF15 deficiency significantly attenuates LPS-induced inflammatory response in vitro and in vivo. Furthermore, DCAF15 interacts with the RBR-type E3 ligase ANKIB1 to form a complex, which promotes KAT5 ubiquitination in a Ser123-dependent manner. Accordingly, ANKIB1 knockdown significantly impairs NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Consequently, KAT5-S123A remarkably decreases NLRP3 acetylation levels and thereby reduces inflammatory responses in vitro and in vivo. Our study uncovers DCAF15‑ANKIB1‑mediated Ser123‑dependent KAT5 ubiquitination as regulator of NLRP3 acetylation and inflammasome activation.

Water Research.title: Acceleration of nitrogen removal from oligotrophic reservoir water: Mechanisms underlying the aerobic denitrification driven by photogenerated electrons.
Water Research.abstract: Carbon limitation and aerobic conditions severely restrict denitrification in oligotrophic reservoir waters. To overcome these constraints, we developed a photoelectrotrophic denitrification (PEDeN) system that utilized photogenerated electrons as an alternative electron source for aerobic denitrifiers, achieving 96% total nitrogen removal within 18 h without an externally applied electrical bias. For the first time, aerobic denitrification outperformed anoxic denitrification in this system, with a total nitrogen removal rate 2.7-fold higher than that under anoxic conditions. This may have resulted from stimulation by the oxygen reduction current, which promoted the secretion of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) containing electron mediators by denitrifying bacteria, thereby enhancing their ability to utilize electrode-derived electrons under aerobic conditions. Moreover, compared with anoxic-light conditions, aerobic-light conditions showed greater metagenomic potential for acetate assimilation, the TCA cycle, cytochrome maturation, and electroactive substance biosynthesis; narG, norB, and nosZ transcript levels were 52.6, 17.5, and 16.0 times those under anoxic-light conditions, respectively. These findings suggested that, under specific electrochemical conditions, aerobic conditions may facilitate the combined utilization of external-circuit electrons and organic carbon through cellular metabolism, thereby improving denitrification performance. This study offers new insights into potential strategies for nitrogen removal in oligotrophic reservoir waters.

Water Research.title: Concentration-Dependent chlorine tolerance despite equivalent CT exposures in multidrug-resistant Stenotrophomonas maltophilia isolate: Associated with putative ribosomal remodeling.
Water Research.abstract: The persistence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) during chlorination challenges water treatment efficacy. We investigated the chlorine tolerance of a newly isolated strain of Stenotrophomonas maltophilia XH by integrating chlorine species and physiological assays with whole-genome, transcriptomic, proteomic, and network analyses. Whole-genome sequencing analysis combined with antibiotic susceptibility testing confirmed that S. maltophilia XH is multidrug-resistant. Concentration-dependent biomolecular defense strategies under equivalent nominal CT (Concentration × Time; 20 mg Cl2·min/L: 1 mg Cl2/L × 20 min vs. 2 mg Cl2/L × 10 min) exposures via multi-omics analysis were first-time comprehensively shown. S. maltophilia XH has high chlorine tolerance. The adaptive strategies of S. maltophilia XH to chlorine were quite distinct from Escherichia coli. Under equivalent nominal CT, distinct exposure dynamics induced different molecular responses. Under 1 mg Cl2/L × 20 min, the bacterium maintained homeostasis primarily through DNA repair and signaling suppression, without apparent cellular oxidative stress responses. Under 2 mg Cl2/L × 10 min, an energy-conserving strategy was revealed: cellular resources were redirected from routine biosynthesis toward membrane repair, ROS detoxification, and extracellular scavenging. A transcriptome-proteome uncoupling response, which could be driven by putative ribosomal remodeling, was observed in S. maltophilia XH. Moreover, this chlorine tolerance strategy concurrently potentiated some macrolide resistance gene expression. Traditional E. coli-based benchmarks could be ineffective against ARB. Effective inactivation could require a high initial chlorine concentration to rapidly breach physiological tolerance thresholds before adaptive networks activate. Additionally, multi-omics demonstrates that transcriptomics alone is insufficient for predicting bacterial responses, and multi-omics analysis provides more information.

Water Research.title: Storage-enabled microbiomes for low-carbon wastewater treatment: Linking carbon capture and retention to electron allocation and process control.
Water Research.abstract: Carbon-limited wastewater treatment is often interpreted as a shortage of biodegradable organic matter, yet treatment performance also depends on when influent carbon is captured, how long it is retained, and how effectively its reducing equivalents are directed to target reactions. Intracellular storage decouples substrate uptake from later electron use by retaining carbon as polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) and glycogen, while polyphosphate cycling supports energy conservation and phosphorus transformations. This Review develops a mechanistic framework for storage-enabled microbiomes in low-C/N wastewater treatment. We distinguish three constraints that can be hidden by similar bulk C/N ratios: insufficient electron inventory, premature carbon loss, and weak coupling between reserve mobilization and terminal respiration. We then connect reserve turnover with central metabolism, respiratory electron carriers, denitrifying reductases, and community-level division of labour. Across post-anoxic denitrification, partial denitrification-anammox, denitrifying phosphorus removal, sulfur-assisted nitrogen removal, and PHA recovery, process performance depends on matching reserve formation, retention, and mobilization with reaction-specific electron and energy demand. We further establish an evidence framework that separates temporal association, stoichiometric plausibility, population or pathway assignment, and perturbation-supported causality. By strengthening intracellular carbon accumulation, preserving reserve-derived electron potential across redox stages and directing subsequent electron release toward target reactions, storage-enabled microbiomes can improve the effective utilization of influent carbon under low-C/N conditions. The engineering benefits of this strategy should be evaluated through nutrient-removal performance, nitrogen-product profiles, N₂O emissions, aeration demand, sulfate and alkalinity balances, sludge production, resource-recovery trade-offs, and disturbance resilience.

Water Research.title: Dynamic coupling and decoupling of odorants and non-CO(2) GHGs during sludge treatment: Associations with EPS redistribution and PFS conditioning.
Water Research.abstract: Sludge treatment units in municipal wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are major sources of nitrogen- and sulfur-containing odorants and non-CO2 greenhouse gases (GHGs). Although odorant and non-CO2 GHG generation are intrinsically coupled via shared anaerobic metabolic pathways, most studies focus on isolated end-of-pipe emissions, leaving their generation profiles and coupling-decoupling mechanisms under thickening and chemical conditioning largely unexplored. Here, we quantified apparent generation rates and stage-specific pollutant loads across the treatment train, including secondary sludge (SS), thickened sludge (TKS), conditioned sludge (CS), and dewatered sludge (DS). The redistribution of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) and physicochemical changes were analyzed to develop a mechanistic interpretation of pollutant generation patterns. The results revealed pronounced stage-specific divergence: odorant generation rates increased from 2.5 to 2.8 μg·kg-1·h-1 in SS/TKS to 46.3-111.4 μg·kg-1·h-1 in CS/DS, while the dominant GHG shifted from CH4 to N2O. Secondary sedimentation, thickening, and conditioning accounted for > 97 % of the total estimated load for each pollutant category. Notably, pollutant generation patterns shifted from coupling in TKS to decoupling following conditioning. In thickened sludge, mild EPS redistribution under neutral anaerobic conditions suggested enhanced substrate bioavailability, helping explain the concurrent increases in odorant and CH4 generation. Polyferric sulfate (PFS) conditioning induced asymmetric EPS redistribution and acidic, sulfate-rich conditions; these changes were associated with a sharp increase in odorant generation, near-complete suppression of biological CH4 generation, and transient N2O release through chemical reactions. These findings associate the observed coupling-decoupling patterns with EPS redistribution and physicochemical changes, informing stage-specific coordinated management of both pollutant categories.

Water Research.title: Physical transport modulates river-sourced OAE efficiency: evidence from an extreme flood in a semi-enclosed estuary.
Water Research.abstract: Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) through river-sourced alkalinity addition has been proposed as a scalable marine carbon dioxide removal strategy, but OAE responses in biogeochemically complex estuaries remain poorly characterized. Using a validated three-dimensional coupled hydrodynamic-biogeochemical model, we examined four prescribed alkalinity increments (+200 to +2000 µmol kg-1) in Yatsushiro Sea during the July 2018 flood. Flood hydrology controlled when and where added alkalinity was delivered, concentrating the perturbation near the surface. For the +500 µmol kg-1 scenario, scaling the CO2-flux response (ΔF) by delivered alkalinity reduced the station-specific R2 for its association with background pCO2 by >94% (residual R2 = 0.004-0.027), indicating that the raw association is strongly linked to differences in delivered alkalinity. The annual delivered-alkalinity-normalized CO2-flux response varied little among doses at St.13 (population coefficient of variation, CV 4.0%) but remained strongly location dependent, with spatial CVs of 58.0%-77.4% at fixed doses. Event-scale carbonate diagnostics showed transient increases in both the Revelle factor and direct total alkalinity sensitivity within the predefined 192-h flood window. At high doses, localized surface Ωaragonite values exceeded the chemical screening line for potential secondary precipitation, identifying a dose-dependent risk that requires site-specific assessment. Together, these results frame extreme floods as favorable delivery windows whose modeled outcomes vary with location, dose, and carbonate state. Because river discharge can be readily measured, discharge-guided dosing provides a practical framework for managing these windows, while precipitation risk and downstream carbon accounting remain priorities for field validation.

Water Research.title: Environmentally relevant antibiotics reduce algal production of the climate-active gas dimethyl sulfide in aquatic ecosystems.
Water Research.abstract: Environmental antibiotics threaten marine climate regulation by disrupting microbial sulfur cycling. As key producers of dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) and its cleavage product dimethylsulfide (DMS), critical drivers of marine cloud formation and climate regulation, dinoflagellates play a pivotal role in global sulfur cycling. This study demonstrates that realistic concentrations (0.1-10 μg/L) of tetracycline (TCs) and sulfadiazine (SDZ) inhibit DMSP and DMS production in marine (Gymnodinium sp.) and freshwater (Peridinium umbonatum) dinoflagellates, despite no observable growth inhibition. Enzymatic assays showed that the activities of DMSP- and DMS-related enzymes (DSYB and DddX) were suppressed under antibiotic exposure in a dose-dependent manner, with TCs exerting stronger inhibitory effects than SDZ. Molecular docking identified stronger TCs-DSYB binding, which may explain its superior enzyme inhibition. Metabolomics uncovered antibiotic-induced sulfur pathway diversion: freshwater species accumulated methionine derivatives, while marine counterparts shifted toward dimethylsulfoxide production, reducing DMS yield by 37-83% in the growth phase. This disruption translates to potential reduction in marine DMS flux. Our findings highlight antibiotics as emerging climate stressors, capable of impairing biogenic cooling mechanisms through enzymatic interference and metabolic rerouting. This study underscores the urgent need to integrate antibiotic pollution into climate models and marine conservation strategies to mitigate unintended climatic consequences.

Water Research.title: Illuminating an overlooked sewage crisis: synthesising evidence on foul waste contamination in surface water sewers across England and Wales.
Water Research.abstract: Separated sewer systems are designed to convey sewage towards treatment facilities while independently directing surface waters into freshwater environments. However, sewer-related issues can lead to foul waste contaminating surface water pipes, which subsequently enters waterbodies via 'Polluted Surface Water Outfalls' (F-PSWOs). Despite creating significant environmental and human health problems globally, F-PSWOs remain overlooked and under-researched. This paper synthesises evidence from England and Wales (United Kingdom) on F-PSWO causes, impacts and management pathways. A novel conceptualisation is presented that details illicit misconnections, failing sewer infrastructure and foul sewer blockages as primary F-PSWO causes. These have been historically examined in silos, but their collective and interactive effects should be more widely investigated. F-PSWO impacts have been sparsely researched, but elevated concentrations of ammonia- and phosphorus-related parameters, increased biochemical oxygen demand and declines in pollution-sensitive taxa have been consistently reported. These trends were broadly supported in new empirical analysis spanning Greater London, where F-PSWOs yielded strong statistical effects on water quality and ecological responses that exceeded Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) influences. This potentially reflects lower CSO densities, but nevertheless indicates that F-PSWOs can be a principal driver of sewage-related impacts in certain freshwater contexts. Finally, F-PSWO management pathways from their original cause to remediation are outlined, including challenges surrounding legal complexities in sewerage governance, monitoring inefficiencies and public (un)awareness, which are discussed alongside emerging opportunities. This study hence sheds much-needed light on this neglected sewage crisis, and highlights the pressing need to protect freshwater ecosystems from the environmental damages caused by F-PSWOs.

Trends in Ecology & Evolution.title: A brief stocktake of the leaf economics spectrum centred on leaf lifespan and specific leaf area
authors: Ian J. Wright, Ülo Niinemets, Peter B. Reich, Mark Westoby
Trends in Ecology & Evolution.abstract: The leaf economics spectrum (LES) was proposed as an analogy linking leaf construction, physiology, lifespan, and ecological strategy. Two decades later, its value lies both in relation to broad-scale trait correlations and to questions those correlations continue to generate. We revisit the LES with emphasis on the leaf lifespan–specific leaf area relationship, a direct expression of the investment–duration trade-off at the heart of leaf economics. Subsequent work has revealed scale dependence from leaves to ecosystems and exposed persistent misunderstandings, such as the assumption that fast-return leaves necessarily imply fast-growing adult plants. Future advances need targeted leaf lifespan data, stronger cost–benefit theory, and more comprehensive tests of how LES relationships shift across environments, ontogeny, and organisational scales.
